1.pericope_label: Miriam and Aaron speak against Moses; the man Moses was very meek

schools.summary: Establish who led the revolt from the text itself. Miriam's name stands first, the verb rendered spake is feminine, and the judgment afterwards fell on her and not on Aaron, who seems to have yielded to her as he had once yielded to the people over the golden calf. Then weigh the identity of the Ethiopian woman without settling for the easy answer. The case for Zipporah has support -- Cushites included an Asiatic division, and a prophet couples Cushan with Midian -- but the wording points to a recent occurrence rather than one more than forty years old, and the murmuring is tied expressly to the woman herself and not to the influence of her relatives; so Zipporah was probably dead. State their claim at face value before it is judged: the high priest who bears the congregation's rights in the Urim and Thummim, and the prophetess, ask whether they too are not organs of divine revelation. Note that the remark that the Lord heard is set down to prepare for his judicial interposition. On the meekness, answer the objection to Mosaic authorship squarely: a later hand may have inserted the verse, but an objective statement of the kind is consistent with true humility, least of all objectionable in men ready to sacrifice their own personality to their cause.

Read the providence in the quarrel before reading the fault. Had Aaron and Miriam always supported their brother, however holy that harmony was, the injustice of many would have alleged it against them as a deceitful and insidious conspiracy; that his own brother and sister contended for the supremacy removed all suspicion of family favour and showed that Moses, opposed by his own belongings, was sustained by the power of God alone. Then name the fault exactly. They pride themselves on a gift of prophecy that ought rather to have schooled them to humility -- such is the depravity of men, not only to abuse God's gifts to the contempt of their brethren, but so to magnify the gifts by ungodly boasting as to obscure the glory of their Author. Aaron's ingratitude is the worse, since the high priesthood had been transferred to him and his descendants while the race of Moses was left in subjection, and still he could not endure being second. On the meekness, treat the parenthesis as explaining why God acted unprompted: the meek man imposed patience on himself and made no complaint, and God nonetheless kept watch. The silence of long-suffering is more effectual before God than any cries.

Separate the ostensible cause from the real one and say which is which. The marriage was the pretext; jealousy of Moses' power and influence was the ground. Observe how little there was to covet -- this government carried no gain and no honour but such as came from God -- and draw the conclusion that the love of power is natural to the human mind, and that men will sacrifice honour, pleasure and profit to it. Note also that because they durst not accuse God they charged Moses his instrument, as the manner of men is. On the woman, allow both readings: Cush in scripture generally means Arabia rather than Ethiopia proper, so Zipporah may be meant, in which case the grievance was not the marriage long past but Moses being swayed by her family in the choice of the seventy elders. Then correct the translation of the third verse. The word rendered meek comes from a root meaning to depress or afflict, so the sense is that Moses was more afflicted than any man of that land, borne down by governing an ungrateful people; the very power they envied was oppressive to its possessor.

Make the point about who these people were, because it is where the sting lies. The trouble came not from enemies but from those eminent in religion, a prophetess and a high priest who had been joint commissioners with Moses for the deliverance of Israel; and from his nearest relations, who shone by rays borrowed from him. A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city. Then turn the same fact into evidence: this helps confirm the call of Moses, showing his advancement was purely of divine favour and not by compact with his kindred, who themselves grudged it -- as neither did many of our Saviour's kindred believe on him. Note how the quarrel spread, Miriam beginning it and Aaron, disgusted at not having been consulted about the seventy elders, drawn in to take his sister's part, as Satan prevailed first with Eve and by her with Adam. We know not how great a matter a little fire may kindle.

debates.question: Who was the Ethiopian woman, and was she the real grievance?

sides.position: Probably not Zipporah. The wording points to a recent occurrence rather than one over forty years old, and the murmuring is tied to the woman herself and not to her relatives' influence; Zipporah was likely dead
Possibly Zipporah, since Cush generally means Arabia rather than Ethiopia proper; if so the quarrel was not the marriage but Moses being swayed by her family in choosing the seventy elders
The marriage was only the ostensible cause; jealousy of Moses' power and influence was the real one, the love of power being natural to the human mind
Perhaps a private falling out between Zipporah and Miriam, one peevish reflection drawing on another until Moses and Aaron were involved

debates.question: Could Moses have written that he was the meekest of men?

sides.position: The objection is unfounded either way. A later hand may have inserted it, but such an objective statement is consistent with true humility, least of all objectionable in men ready to sacrifice their own personality to their cause
The word is misunderstood. Its root means to depress or afflict, so the sense is that Moses was more afflicted than any man of that land, borne down by governing an ungrateful people
A later hand is likely, Joshua or Ezra under the same inspiration; it is a testimony from God, not a self-commendation
Probably added by some succeeding prophet; and since we often read of Moses in anger, it only proves that the law made nothing perfect

outliers.note: Alone finds a providence in the quarrel itself, arguing that had Aaron and Miriam always supported their brother the harmony would have been alleged against them as a deceitful conspiracy, so that their opposition removed all suspicion of family favour and showed Moses upheld by the power of God alone.

Alone rejects the received translation of the third verse, taking the word from a root meaning to depress or afflict and reading it that Moses was more afflicted than any man of that land, since the very power they envied was oppressive to its possessor.

themes: Miriam and Aaron spake against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married
Hath the LORD indeed spoken only by Moses? hath he not spoken also by us? And the LORD heard it
the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth

4.pericope_label: Come out ye three; with him will I speak mouth to mouth

schools.summary: Explain first why the summons was so sudden, and give both reasons: God acted as one greatly provoked, and he acted before the complaint could spread among a people already disposed to mutiny; the speed also proves that Moses had not solicited it, no time being allowed him to apply. Then let the place do part of the work. They are called to the tabernacle so that the sanctity of it may cast down a haughtiness grown out of forgetfulness of God, and separated from Moses so that they may confess an inferiority they had denied. On the modes of revelation be exact about the word. The term is not the one meaning a prophecy but the one expressing a visible appearance, which ratifies the truth of God's word to the eyes and all the senses; such sights were frequent to the patriarchs before the Law. The point of naming the two ordinary modes is to withdraw Moses from the common condition by a special privilege. Note how the apostle uses the clause about faithfulness in God's house to prove Moses inferior to Christ, a servant and member of the church against its Lord and builder. And when the cloud departs, remember that God who fills all things never moves from his place; the name is applied metaphorically to the symbol of his presence.

Begin from what Moses did not do. He did not resent the injury, complain of it, or appeal to God; God resented it for him. Draw the lesson at once, since it is the practical use of the whole passage: God hears all we say in our passion and is a swift witness of hasty speeches, which is reason to bridle our tongues about others and to stop our ears when others speak ill of us. The more silent we are in our own cause, the more God is engaged to plead it; an innocent man need say little when the judge himself will be his advocate. Then stage the scene as a trial. Judges of old sat in the gate of the city to try causes, and here the glory stands at the door of the tabernacle while the accused are called to the bar. Moses had often shown himself jealous for God's honour, and now God shows himself jealous for his reputation, for those that honour God he will honour.

Guard the details of the scene against over-reading. Nothing here implies that Miriam entered the tabernacle itself: the three were summoned out of the camp to the entrance of the court, there being only one court at this time, and the further command to approach the sanctuary came afterwards. Improve the rendering where the English obscures the sense -- if there be among you a prophet of Jehovah, noting that the Greek and Latin versions attach the divine name to the earlier clause; not so in regard to my servant Moses, he is faithful; and with him do I speak, mouth to mouth. Take the word rendered apparently as denoting an objective reality rather than an inward vision, the same noun that elsewhere means a sight; and note that the word rendered similitude is the term of the second commandment, the two standing together in a verse of Job. Observe finally that the contrast drawn here between Moses as servant in God's house and Christ as Son over his own house is the one the Epistle to the Hebrews takes up.

Take the suddenness as itself an index: the interference shows at once the importance of the case and the displeasure, and it stifled the sedition before it could spread. Read the command to come out as a summons from their private dwellings to learn God's pleasure and their own doom, and mark that they were kept standing at the door rather than admitted as Aaron was accustomed to be, which is a further sign of displeasure. State the conclusion the passage forces without softening it: if they are prophets, still there is a difference among prophets, and God does not put equal honour on all. Supply the reason Moses could not be dealt with in enigmas -- he was to receive laws whose precepts must be within reach of the meanest capacity. Then gloss the mode of his revelation carefully: distinct and articulate speech, not by an interpreter nor by shadows in the fancy, and not in the dark speeches given to others, the boiling pot shown to Jeremiah or the chariot to Ezekiel. Deny that he saw the essence of God, which no man can see and live, and propose a singular manifestation of glory instead, the Son appearing in a human shape taken up for the time as a foretaste of the incarnation. And end where the verse ends: the removal of God's presence is the saddest token of his displeasure, and he never departs till we drive him off.

debates.question: Why was the summons so sudden?

sides.position: Because God was greatly provoked, and to stop the complaint spreading among a people disposed to mutiny; the speed also proved Moses had not solicited it
To stifle the beginnings of the sedition before it reached the people
The suddenness shows at once the importance of the case and the displeasure
So that the sanctity of the place might cast down a haughtiness grown out of forgetfulness of God

debates.question: What is meant by the similitude of the Lord?

sides.position: Not the essence of God, which no man can see and live, but a singular manifestation of glory; the Son appeared in a human shape taken up for the time as a foretaste of the incarnation
The word is the term of the second commandment, standing beside its companion in a verse of Job; the noun rendered apparently denotes an objective reality rather than an inward vision

outliers.note: Alone draws the practical rule from Moses' silence, that the more silent we are in our own cause the more God is engaged to plead it, and that an innocent man need say little when the judge himself will be his advocate.

Alone guards the staging of the scene, insisting that nothing here implies Miriam entered the tabernacle itself, since the three were called only to the entrance of the court, there being but one court at this time.

themes: Come out ye three unto the tabernacle of the congregation
If there be a prophet among you, I the LORD will make myself known unto him in a vision
With him will I speak mouth to mouth, even apparently, and not in dark speeches

10.pericope_label: Miriam leprous as snow; Aaron's plea; Heal her now, O God

schools.summary: Put the sequence first and let it stand as a maxim: the cloud departed, and Miriam became leprous; when God goes, evil comes, and expect no good when God departs. Then set this stroke among its fellows. Leprosy was often inflicted by the immediate hand of God as the punishment of a particular sin -- on Gehazi for lying, on Uzziah for invading the priest's office, and here on Miriam for making mischief among relations. Let the punishment be seen to fit: a foul tongue justly punished with a foul face, and her pretension to rival Moses made manifest to all, since everyone sees his face glorious and hers leprous, so that while Moses needs a veil to hide his glory, Miriam needs one to hide her shame. Draw the application to the reader from that: distempers that deform us ought to be construed as a rebuke to pride, and it is a sign the heart is hard indeed if the flesh be mortified and the lusts of the flesh remain unmortified. Then explain the sparing of Aaron -- God would put a difference between those that mislead and those that are misled, and his office secured him from a token that would have suspended his service and left a lasting blot on his family.

Attend to what Aaron does under the blow, since it is the measure of the change in him. Knowing that his own punishment had been remitted by indulgence, he does not cease to consider what he had deserved; when God chastises others he invites us to repentance, and we should profit by their punishments without waiting to be struck ourselves. The dread of punishment was the best medicine for his disease of ambition -- he now calls the younger brother whose superiority he lately could not endure his lord, and confesses himself subject to him. Note that in begging Moses not to impute the sin he does not usurp for a mortal a right God claims for himself alone, but asks pardon of one he had injured. Note too that he does not extenuate, as most people do, covering a transgression under the plea of error or thoughtlessness; he says plainly that they were senseless. Then explain the physical detail without flinching from it: she was as one dead in a ceremonial sense, shut out and defiling by touch, and in a natural sense her flesh had become as dead flesh, which unless miraculously cured must have ended in her death.

Mark that the cloud's going is described by a different word from the one used when it is taken up for a march: the lifting was the signal to break camp, this was the token of a presence and a guidance withdrawn. On the disease, render it was leprous as snow, and note the rule this case breaks -- when leprosy covered the whole body and all the flesh turned white the man was pronounced clean, but it was otherwise where the stroke came immediately from God, as with the hand of Moses and with Gehazi. Observe that Aaron turned toward his sister, and that this may have been the first occasion on which he had to carry out the law of inspection laid down for the priests. On Aaron's plea, take the word rendered alas as an exclamation of entreaty rather than lamentation, used toward superiors, and read the request as asking not that the guilt be shifted but that they be spared the punishment it deserved. Report that the scribes are said to have altered the text of the comparison with the dead child, and give the severer original. Then defend the unusual construction of Moses' prayer against those who would emend it, since the proposed alteration yields no fitting sense.

Be precise about what moved and what did not: the cloud left not the whole tabernacle but the part it had come to, returning to its place over the mercy-seat. Explain why she and not Aaron, giving both reasons -- she was chief in the transgression, and God would not have his worship interrupted or dishonoured, which it must have been had the high priest been leprous. Add the harder application, since it is the one that costs: how many priests and preachers who deserved exposure have been spared for the sake of the holy character they bore, that the ministry might not be blamed; but the just God will visit their transgressions some other way if they do not deeply deplore them. Nothing discredits the work of God so much as the miscarriages of those who minister in holy things. On the leprosy, note that this kind was the most virulent and incurable, precisely because the whiteness came suddenly rather than by degrees; and make the comparison with the dead child concrete -- a still-born infant that has lain some time in the womb and comes forth putrefied.

debates.question: Why was Miriam struck and not Aaron?

sides.position: God would put a difference between those that mislead and those that are misled; and Aaron's office secured him from a token that would have suspended his service and blotted his family

Had the high priest been smitten his sacred character must have suffered and the priesthood fallen into contempt -- as ministers are still spared exposure for the sake of the office, though God visits their transgressions another way
Either because she was chief in the transgression, or because God would not have his worship interrupted or dishonoured
Because she was first in the transgression and so alone punished, while Aaron was drawn in, confessed, and was forgiven

debates.question: What does leprous as snow signify here?

sides.position: Not the ordinary case: a whiteness covering the whole body would have meant the man was clean, but not where the stroke came immediately from God, as with the hand of Moses and with Gehazi
The most virulent and incurable kind, precisely because the whiteness came suddenly rather than by degrees
A punishment fitted to the offence, a foul tongue punished with a foul face, so that Moses needs a veil to hide his glory and Miriam one to hide her shame

outliers.note: Alone turns the sparing of Aaron on the reader, observing how many priests and preachers who deserved exposure have been spared for the sake of the character they bore, and warning that the just God will visit their transgressions some other way.

Alone reads Aaron's plea as evidence that his ambition was cured, noting that he now calls a younger brother his lord, and that he refuses to extenuate the fault under the plea of thoughtlessness as most people do.

themes: the cloud departed from off the tabernacle; and, behold, Miriam became leprous, white as snow
lay not the sin upon us, wherein we have done foolishly, and wherein we have sinned
Heal her now, O God, I beseech thee

14.pericope_label: Shut out from the camp seven days; the people journeyed not

schools.summary: Explain the figure from the custom: spitting in a person's presence, still more in the face, counts in the East as the extreme sign of abhorrence and indignation, and the clause may be rendered in her presence. Then answer why seven days from the leprosy law itself, where seven is both the period a suspected leper is shut up in the first instance and the period a cleansed leper tarries outside his tent before the sacrifices are offered for him. State the reversal plainly: the woman who had put herself on a level with the divinely appointed head of the nation was excluded for seven days from privileges the humblest member of the congregation enjoyed. Make the proportion explicit -- in exaggerating the worth of her own prophetic gift she had exalted herself above the congregation, and was struck with the one disease that puts a person outside the number of the people of God -- and note that the sentence carried its own limit, restoration and cleansing being promised once the seven days were endured. On the resumed march, identify the encampment in Paran with Kadesh, near a spring on the heights south of Beersheba.

Draw the argument the comparison implies. A father spat in a child's face only under great provocation, and the child was then banished from his presence for seven days; if such severity was allowed between child and parent, it can hardly be excessive where a creature has rebelled against the Creator. Press what the sentence cost rather than its length: to be shut out of the camp was to be debarred from the presence of God, who is represented as dwelling among the people, and to a soul that knows the blessedness of communion with him seven days of such darkness would be intolerable. Take the shame to mean withdrawing oneself, as Jonathan withdrew from his father's table, and note that though God healed her at Moses' request he would have her publicly bear the shame of her sin as a warning to others. Read the nation's waiting as respect rather than delay, ordered so that she should not be overwhelmed by so public a rebuke and so that the gift of prophecy should not fall into contempt through her. And take the long view from that camp: a journey of a few weeks became thirty-eight years, so much ground may be lost in the divine life by a single act of unfaithfulness.

Keep cure and punishment distinct, because the text does not join them. Miriam was no doubt healed at once; the exclusion that followed was penalty and not treatment, and in later times lepers dwelt alone only so long as the disease was on them. Explain the mechanics of what follows without embroidery: the cloud returned to the tabernacle and was taken up again, which was the signal for motion, and the camps of Israel removed in their order. Locate the next station and date it -- eight miles from Hazeroth on one authority, and reached toward the end of the third month. Then note what the place became. Israel was now very near the promised land and might quickly have entered it; it was the affair of the spies sent from this camp that kept them out thirty-eight years longer. Note also that the divine word here may have come by a voice out of the cloud at a distance, or by a secret impulse darting such words into the mind as if an audible voice had spoken.

debates.question: What force has the comparison with a father spitting?

sides.position: It is the extreme eastern sign of abhorrence and indignation, and the clause may be rendered in her presence
It is an argument from the lesser: if seven days' banishment was allowed a provoked parent, the punishment can hardly be excessive where a creature has rebelled against the Creator
It means an eminent token of indignation, the shame consisting in withdrawing oneself as Jonathan withdrew from his father's table
It means keeping herself hidden out of pure shame

debates.question: Why did the whole nation wait for her?

sides.position: As a testimony of respect from God and the people, ordered so that she should not be overwhelmed by so public a rebuke and so that the gift of prophecy should not fall into contempt
Simply because they did not proceed until her restoration was complete
Because the cloud had to return to the tabernacle and be taken up again before there was any signal for motion

outliers.note: Alone explains why the nation waited, giving two reasons for God so ordering it, that Miriam should not be overwhelmed by so public a rebuke, and that the gift of prophecy should not fall into contempt through her.

Alone derives the seven days from the leprosy law itself, where seven is both the period a suspected leper is shut up and the period a cleansed leper tarries outside his tent before the sacrifices are offered for him.

themes: If her father had but spit in her face, should she not be ashamed seven days?
let her be shut out from the camp seven days, and after that let her be received in again
the people journeyed not till Miriam was brought in again
